512.completion:
the steady hum of traffic and the cries of hawks overhead. Most often, he listened to all the sounds that slipped into his room through the open window. This particular sound, something he had never heard before then, disturbed rather than soothed him.
"Owen, what are you doing?"
Oh; it was his mum in the doorway. Every thought he tried to entertain faded away as soon as he saw her. He felt himself pulled into her orbit, even as the effort felt draining from him. The grey eyes and black hair; she was his mother.
"Silly boy."
"Missis, I have to talk to you," said Owen, knowing he didn't. "I've got the money, now give me the drugs."
"Fool," said Kathryn, brows lined with old pains, "you know I can't. You think I don't wish I could? I wish you had never found me at all. Oh, my beautiful boy, you are angry with me."
Owen felt his anger fade away. He couldn't be angry with her, not as long as she was the image of the woman he loved. How could he hurt someone who loved him so? He didn't want to murder the old woman, the person he once loved, now withered by the streets she inhabited.
"No, Missis, I can't be angry," said Owen, helplessly. "I love you too much."
"Oh, my love," said Kathryn, "my poor boy. Your eyes are so broken."
"And I still want the drugs," said Owen, "so please."
"I can't do that without hurting you, and I love you too much."
"Missis, let me ask you something, then."
"What?"
"What would you say to having a son who talks to animals?"
"Ah, boy, I know they talk, and I know I can understand them, that's true. They speak of the future, but they lie and say it is the past."
"Missis, is that why you've stopped eating their sacrifices to you?"
"Don't talk about that."
"Because there's no future, is it? The rabbit said we'd be dead and I was supposed to tell you, but it was lying?"
"Yes, it was lying," she said hopelessly. "The future is full of death. Stop listening to those fools!"
